climate.koppen_name: Cold, no dry season, warm summer

climate: Seasons this mild ripen Pinot Gris, Gewürztraminer, Riesling, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay fully without cooking off their freshness.

soil.rock: Loess is fine, wind-blown silt. Fertile and warm, it holds water well but drains poorly.
soil.top: The topsoil holds water well and drains at a steady pace, so vines rarely go thirsty or sit in wet ground. Its pH is close to neutral, so vines take up the nutrients they need easily.

land: The high ground runs about 3°F cooler than the low ground. Higher vineyards ripen later and keep more acidity, so one grape can make lighter or richer wine here depending on height.
Gentle slopes. Enough tilt to drain cold air and rain away, which lowers frost risk, yet still easy to farm by machine.

sheet.place: Tokaj is a hilly wine region in northeast Hungary. Volcanic rock sits under clay and loess. Two rivers, the Bodrog and the Tisza, bring autumn mist that helps noble rot grow. UNESCO listed the landscape in 2002.
sheet.rules: A 1737 royal decree closed the Tokaj region to outsiders. Szamorodni is made from whole bunches that include some noble rot. It can be sweet (édes) or dry (száraz). Aszú is the richer style, made from hand-picked rotted berries.
sheet.dulo: A dűlő is a named vineyard site. The name on the label tells you the wine comes from that one plot.
sheet.hatalos: Hatalos is a hill near Szegi and Szegilong. The Kvaszinger plot is about 3 hectares at 300 metres. The soil is clay with broken rock over volcanic bedrock.

claims.claim: Tokaj is a protected wine region in northeast Hungary, in the Hegyalja foothills of the Zemplén hills. A small part lies in Slovakia and uses the same name.

The Hungarian wine region has 27 settlements: Tokaj, Abaújszántó, Bekecs, Bodrogkeresztúr, Bodrogkisfalud, Bodrogolaszi, Erdőbénye, Erdőhorváti, Golop, Hercegkút, Legyesbénye, Mád, Makkoshotyka, Mezőzombor, Monok, Olaszliszka, Rátka, Sárazsadány, Sárospatak, Sátoraljaújhely, Szegi, Szegilong, Szerencs, Tállya, Tarcal, Tolcsva and Vámosújfalu.
Planted area is about 5,500 ha. Classified vineyard land is about 11,149 ha.
Tokaj was made a closed wine region (zárt borvidék) in 1737 and is often called the first in the world. English Wikipedia says the royal decree was 1737 or 1757.

The vineyards were ranked in classes: first growth, second growth and third growth, with a top 'great first growth' tier for a few sites such as Mézes Mály. Many named vineyards in the old ranking are no longer planted.
UNESCO listed the Tokaj Wine Region Historic Cultural Landscape as a World Heritage Site in 2002, under criteria (iii) and (v). The core zone is 13,255 ha.
The bedrock is volcanic: rhyolite and andesite and their tuffs. Topsoils are clay or loess over this. Weathered volcanic material forms a dark loam-type soil called nyirok.

Loess is deepest around Tokaj and Tarcal, up to about 20 m on the far side of the Tarcal hill. Loess sites tend to give softer wines. Volcanic clay sites such as Mád give more mineral, higher-acid wines.
The best vineyards are on sunny, mostly south-facing slopes of the hills.
The Bodrog and Tisza rivers meet beside the town of Tokaj. Their humidity plus autumn mist and sunny days favour botrytis (noble rot), which dries the grapes on the vine.
Six varieties are permitted: Furmint, Hárslevelű, Sárgamuskotály (yellow muscat), Zéta, Kövérszőlő and Kabar.

Furmint is the main grape and keeps high acidity, suits noble rot and ages well. Hárslevelű (linden leaf) gives linden-honey notes and less acidity, and is planted lower on slopes. Sárgamuskotály is muscat-scented and rarely makes aszú.
Kabar is Bouvier x Hárslevelű, and Zéta (formerly Oremus) is Bouvier x Furmint, bred in 1951.
Furmint is roughly 60 to 70 percent of plantings, Hárslevelű roughly 25 to 30 percent and Sárgamuskotály roughly 5 percent.

Szamorodni is made from whole bunches that include a good share of botrytised grapes, so it is fuller and higher in alcohol than ordinary wine. Sweet (édes) versions can hold about 100 to 120 g/L residual sugar. With fewer botrytised berries it ends up dry (száraz), around 14% alcohol.
The UK register says Szamorodni must is at least 230.2 g/L sugar and the wine is aged at least two years, one of them in barrel. It must carry the Tokaj PDO.

Aszú is made from individually picked botrytised berries kneaded into a paste (aszú dough). Must or wine is poured over the paste and left 24 to 48 hours, then the wine ferments and ages slowly in cask.

Aszú used to be graded 3 to 6 puttonyos by how many baskets of aszú paste went into each cask. Since the 2013 harvest every aszú needs at least 120 g/L residual sugar. The 2026 amendment is reported to set 18 months minimum in cask.
Late harvest (késői szüretelésű) wines are reductive sweet wines made without the aszú process, ready 1 to 18 months after harvest, with 50 to 180 g/L residual sugar.

Other traditional styles are eszencia (free-run juice from aszú berries, 500 to 700 g/L sugar, about 5 to 6% alcohol), fordítás (must poured over used aszú paste) and máslás (must poured over aszú lees). A search summary says the 2026 amendment drops aszúeszencia, dry fordítás and dry máslás.
Dry Tokaj is made from the same grapes without the sweet-wine processes. The 2022 vintage rules for dry wine were not found.
Hegyalja means 'foothills' and was the region's old name. 'Tokaj' may come from an Old Turkic word for 'forest by a river' or from a Slavic word for a confluence. 'Tokaji' just means 'of Tokaj'.

A dűlő is a named vineyard site, a defined plot of land with its own name and history. In Tokaj, historic dűlők were ranked in the old classification. A producer can print the name on the label for a single-site wine.

Hatalos is a hill on the edge of Szegi and Szegilong. Kvaszinger's winery address is in Szegilong. The Grand Tokaj Szegi Cellar is cut into the volcanic Hatalos hill, a system of roughly 400-year-old rock quarries over 5 km long.
Kvaszinger's Hatalos soil is clay mixed with broken rock over volcanic bedrock.
Kvaszinger's Hatalos Furmint plot is about 3 ha, planted in 1998, at about 300 m. Merchant listings describe the Hatalos vineyard as south or south-east facing.
The Kvaszinger family bought its first vineyard, Hatalos, in 1929.

Hatalos soil is described by the producer's importers only. No geological survey or classification entry was found.

No rule text was read for dry Tokaj, late harvest or édes Szamorodni sugar minimums.
